Entre la jungle et le système : la santé: Between the Jungle and the System: The Mental Health of Asylum Seekers at Roxham Road
« Je suis un homme marié, père de trois: “I’m a married man, a father of three children, one of whom was born in Canada. I came here looking for a better life”
Louis Salomon, un demandeur d'asile ayan: Louis Salomon, an asylum seeker who came through Roxham Road, recounts his journey; he is still haunted by his migration story. Illustration: Nia E-K
Tout risquer pour partir en quête d’une: Risking everything in search of a better life: these are the words often used to describe the stories of migrants who travel thousands of kilometres and use routes like Roxham Road to enter Canada. Once on Canadian soil, newcomers face problems that test their physical and material well-being. Mental health is rarely mentioned when people talk about these exiles, and neither is the question of well-being. But how does an irregular crossing through so many territories affect the mental health of asylum seekers, and what does the system offer to help them? La Converse looked into the question as Roxham Road <l1>is about to close.</l1>
« Je suis un homme marié, père de trois: “I’m a married man, a father of three children, one of whom was born in Canada. I came here looking for a better life,” Louis Salomon tells us. His introduction is interrupted by another thought: “Before Canada, on my way here, there were tragic nights I can’t shake.” His thoughts seem scattered, memories jostling in his mind, and he starts talking about what he went through. “I spent two nights in the Mexican forest. I saw bodies hanging from trees, emptied of their organs. There were wild animals, jaguars, pumas and birds that eat flesh,” Louis lists hurriedly. Benjamin, the trainee deacon who is accompanying him, is shocked by this revelation; he had no idea.
C’est par un chaud vendredi de juillet q: It was on a hot Friday in July that the Salomons set out on a perilous odyssey through seven countries in barely a month. They crossed Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras, Guatemala and Mexico. Arriving near the border between the first two countries, they spent five days crossing the Darién Gap, one of the most unforgiving and deadly jungles in the world. It was there that Louis had a macabre encounter that will stay etched in his memory forever. “I found a man lying on the ground and I put my ear to his chest. He was almost dead, but his heart was still beating,” he explains. Despite his exhaustion, he lifted the stranger onto his shoulders, but he couldn’t carry him like that for very long. “My wife was pregnant and also needed my support,” he says. He says he found himself facing a hard choice: abandon the man or risk the life of his own family. “In the end I decided to hide the man behind a rock, hoping he might survive,” he says in a breathless voice. “I had barely walked away when wild animals appeared and attacked the man, who was still alive,” he confides, lowering his head and avoiding our gaze.
Louis poursuit son récit. Il nous confie: Louis continues his story. He tells us he will never forget the night of August 14, 2021. He was in Mexico. He and 150 other Haitian migrants were waiting for the Senda De Vida church to take them to Reynosa, a border city. His wife, being pregnant, had already left the area with another group deemed a priority. Around 1 a.m., while the group was still waiting, police burst in to deport them. In a panic, Louis and nine others ran to take refuge in the forest. Their fear quickly turned to horror when they discovered 12 bodies hanging from trees. A witness to unimaginable violence, Louis says: “I can’t erase that scene from my memory.” Only he and another survivor named Jean made it through this ordeal; the others ended up in the jaws of wild animals. Even today, Louis says, the experience haunts him.
Sauvé in extremis par des hélicoptères,: Saved at the last minute by helicopters, he found his wife again after two nightmarish nights. Their ordeal was not over, however. Three months later, Louis, temporarily settled in Mexico, obtained a humanitarian letter granting him a psychological consultation in the United States. The Salomons finally reached the Texas border, only to be handed a deportation letter issued without the slightest consideration. They then spent a month at the home of Louis’s older sister in the United States and managed to scrape together enough money for the last leg of the journey to Canada. Exhausted and traumatized, Louis and his wife finally boarded a bus headed for the Canadian border, hoping at last to find refuge and a better life.
Le stress, ce fléau aux multiples visage: Stress, that many-faced scourge, consumes Louis a little more each day. Everything he feels, whether fear or sadness, he ties to stress. He falls into trance-like states that he struggles to come out of, and his wife, desperate, sometimes tries to bring him back to reality. “Who are you trying to hit? Do you know where you are? We’re in Montréal,” he recounts, whipping his hand through the air as a demonstration. He has only disconnected murmurs to offer in response: “I’m not here, not really,” moans the Montréal-Nord resident. Even his love for his wife is smothered by this invisible enemy gnawing at him from the inside. Too overwhelmed by stress, he can no longer show her affection. “Every loud noise, every cry from my little girl, her tears or her joy, makes my heart pound and brings on cold sweats,” says the father bitterly.
Arrivés au Canada, les Salomon sont conf: Upon arriving in Canada, the Salomons were confronted with a new and harsh reality. The first Canadians they met were employees of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Louis says that during that first exchange he sensed a coldness in them as icy as the winter that welcomed them. Yet that was nothing compared to the isolation and distress he felt once across the border. “I feel completely lost here. I don’t know who to turn to… I went to PRAIDA (Programme régional d’accueil et d’intégration des demandeurs d’asile) twice. The first time, they gave me a transit pass and a meagre $50 allowance. The second time, they told me to wait for social assistance, but my daughter needed milk. I went home empty-handed. I was so stressed, I couldn’t sleep anymore,” laments the 47-year-old, left to fend for himself.
En décembre dernier, l’anxiété lui a coû: Last December, anxiety cost him his job at the Efficacité agency. “I was working and I couldn’t stop thinking about my children in Haiti, especially my youngest son, who needed money to pay his school fees,” he says, in despair. As he brooded, an intense pain seized him. He then realized that a nail had lodged itself in his thumb. The ambulance, the hospital, and finally time off work: all of it because of the anguish that had overwhelmed him. “When I’m alone, thoughts flood my mind and the stress overwhelms me,” he adds, describing his anxiety. His work contract was due to end a week later, but the accident cut his employment short. Since then, Louis Salomon has been unemployed. This has been going on for months.
Ce qui alimente son angoisse, c’est le m: What feeds his anguish is the lack of resources and information. “The police, the paperwork, the delays: everything is new to me. I feel more alone than ever, facing a system that seems hostile and incomprehensible to me. I had to go to a hearing last month because I wasn’t able to submit my Basis of Claim (BOC) on time. The judge could have told me I was accepted or refused in Canada and I wouldn’t have understood a thing,” he says, shaken.
Au même moment, il ne pouvait s’empêcher: At the same time, he couldn’t help asking himself: “Why so much stress? Why so much anguish? Don’t they know we’re already vulnerable? I just want to live legally.” Looking at his friend Benjamin, Louis adds: “In Canada, I’ve found only Frantz André to help me. He’s the one who helped me fill out the documents I needed for my BOC. It’s also thanks to him that I met Benjamin Ntouo-Ngouoni, who drove me here today and bought milk for my daughter yesterday.”
Cette désinformation a induit Louis en e: This misinformation has misled Louis more than once. Not long ago, he gave up his right to social assistance for fear of going into debt, even though he can’t find work. “I like to work, I like to earn my living and provide for my family. Last week I went around to nine placement agencies, and they told me there would be work in March, but no, there’s nothing. My fellow Haitians warned me that if I didn’t stop taking social assistance, I’d end up in debt. I don’t know what to do anymore, I don’t know how to feed my family,” the asylum seeker explains to us.
La déconnexion, l’angoisse, le manque d’: The disconnection, the anguish, the lack of focus and the inability to sleep are only symptoms of a deeper ailment. His suffering is the consequence of a system that struggles to serve asylum seekers. Louis pulls three cards out of his wallet: two residency cards (one from Chile and the other from Brazil), then says that “the third card is a medical access card – in Brazil everyone has the right to health care.”
Pour un homme qui a d’énormes responsabi: For a man with enormous responsibilities, Louis admits he wants access to a psychologist. “I think it could help us, me and my wife,” he concludes.
<strong>« Le Canada ne lui a pas ouvert: “Canada didn’t open the front door for him, so he came in through the window”
Travailleur social depuis plus d’une déc: A social worker for more than a decade, Vincent Richard has held several positions at PRAIDA over the past six years. “There’s a tendency to downplay what Roxham Road is, to believe these are people who show up in a taxi and cross the border with a whole setup waiting to welcome them,” says the housing team leader.
Le caractère irrégulier du passage par l: The irregular nature of the crossing at Roxham Road has a major impact on the mental health of the people who have made it. “Most people who take this route are forced to make a long journey across the Americas, passing through ten or even fifteen borders before arriving in Canada,” he exclaims. For the Salomons, for example, the trip was especially hard, with 13 countries crossed. He explains that people who cross the Canada–U.S. border from the United States can’t present themselves at an official port of entry because of the Safe Third Country Agreement. “An asylum seeker once told me that Canada didn’t open the front door for him, so he came in through the window. Getting to Canada this way costs a great deal financially, physically and psychologically,” Richard adds.
Une fois au pays, ces personnes sont arr: Once in the country, these people are arrested and sometimes detained for further checks. “That doesn’t create a welcoming situation; it causes anguish from the very first contact,” continues the social worker, who has worked in welcoming asylum seekers. “Despite all the explanations we give them, many still consider themselves illegal people.”
Pour M. Richard, il est important de com: For Richard, it’s important to understand that every asylum seeker has a unique background and that the issues differ from one person to the next. He notes, however, that many of them suffer from depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder. “They’re often in survival mode for a prolonged period, and once they’re safe in Canada, their defence mechanisms collapse and their traumas resurface,” he explains with empathy.
« Naviguer dans un nouveau système n’est: “Navigating a new system isn’t easy for anyone, let alone for people who have been forcibly displaced for safety reasons,” the support worker points out. He says he has witnessed newcomers’ worry, fear and shame about their status. And among those who had to leave loved ones behind, guilt and grief can turn into suicidal thoughts.
« Le système n’offre pas des possibilité: “The system doesn’t offer equal opportunities. For example, asylum seekers aren’t funded for French-language courses, unlike permanent residents. As a result, many have to make a sacrifice: a job or communication. The consequences of their choice, whichever it is, show in their integration,” adds Vincent Richard. According to the social worker, the lack of accurate and precise information worsens the feeling of uprootedness and the sense of confusion. “There’s misinformation within ethnocultural communities and a misunderstanding of the asylum process. The process isn’t easy to understand, even for those who work in the field. It stems from a systemic failure of accessibility and creates situations of precarity that take a toll on their mental health and hinder their integration into the host society,” he explains.
Toujours à propos des inégalités du syst: Still on the subject of the system’s inequalities mentioned earlier, he elaborates: “There are many orderlies of Haitian origin who were or are asylum seekers. They take care of our elderly and fill essential jobs that others refuse to do. Despite their contribution, they are often underestimated and seen as people taking advantage of the system by a general public that is ignorant of the reality of asylum seekers. They’re reduced to statistics and dollars, forgetting the human being behind every asylum story. In reality, even though they have access to social assistance, they try to get off it as quickly as possible. They’re not proud to live from one paycheque to the next, barely able to make ends meet. They want to work and enter the job market to contribute to the host society,” he reminds us.
Ces représentations affectent leur intég: These perceptions affect their integration into society, because “we also have to acknowledge that there’s a problem of systemic racism. For example, discrimination in access to housing. It’s easier for a Vincent than for a Mamadou to get an apartment,” says the Quebecer.
Garine Papazian-Zohrabian, la directrice: Garine Papazian-Zohrabian, scientific director of the Équipe de recherche interdisciplinaire sur les familles réfugiées et demandeuses d’asile, points out that the realities of refugees and asylum seekers in Canada are very different. Refugees are selected by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in predetermined neighbouring countries, and then automatically receive permanent residence once they arrive at the airport. “That allows them to live in better conditions in Canada,” she explains.
Pour ce qui est des demandeurs d’asile,: For asylum seekers, arriving in Canada is only the start of a long, anxiety-inducing process. “First there’s the anguish of entering irregularly (for example, through Roxham Road) and the absence of a warm welcome. Then they have to prove there is a real danger of death for them in their country of origin,” she explains. The researcher says the federal government’s first response to an asylum claim should come within three months of the initial application. “Right now, the system is so overloaded that claimants sometimes wait up to 15 months for a first answer, which creates uncertainty for them, because files can be rejected and people deported,” adds Papazian-Zohrabian.
Le manque de stabilité que confère un st: The lack of stability that comes with permanent status dictates the lives of asylum seekers. “There’s a lot of precarity tied to this status. These people don’t have access to the same health services. Only children under 18 are entitled to free schooling. The wait for a work permit is too long. Access to child care is nonexistent, which limits their job options. All of this worsens their living conditions […] It leads to mental health problems, particularly anxiety, among people seeking asylum,” the researcher continues.
Par ailleurs, l’environnement dans leque: Furthermore, the environment in which asylum seekers live plays a major role in their psychological recovery and their integration into the host society. Papazian-Zohrabian, who is also a professor of psychoeducation at Université de Montréal, points out that political decisions can strongly influence the atmosphere around them. “Section 15 of Bill 96, adopted by the National Assembly, which concerns all immigrants, prohibits the use of any language other than French six months after their arrival. It poses a major problem for people in financial precarity, who can’t afford interpreters. This situation creates problems of access to information, legal services and health care.”
Malgré tout, la psychologue affirme qu’e: Despite everything, the psychologist says she doesn’t take a defeatist view of asylum seekers’ mental health. She insists: “Yes, their mental health can recover; everything depends on their post-migration living conditions, the welcome and the integration services they receive.” She reminds us that “these people have already survived many difficult situations before arriving here and that they have as many areas of strength as of vulnerability.” “When we talk about trauma, we’re also talking about survival, about creativity. Asylum seekers find ways to adapt, develop strategies to get back up and keep going. This ability to adapt helps them integrate into the host society,” she says.
L’un des moyens de soutenir ce processus: One way to support this recovery process is to create creative spaces that allow people to symbolize and express their experiences and traumas without relying on language – what Garine Papazian-Zohrabian calls a “healing process.”
De la peinture, des crayons, des feuille: Paint, pencils, sheets of paper and colouring books are spread across the table at the Centre de réfugiés (CDR) at la Ruche artistique. With citizens, newcomers and staff, the creative process begins.
Miguel, un demandeur d’asile qui sort d’: Miguel, an asylum seeker fresh from a session with the legal department, picks up coloured pencils and an empty folder and sets out on an ambitious mission to turn beige into a rainbow. “So many people are sitting around this table, and no one speaks the same language. But we keep drawing, colouring, expressing ourselves. By showing each other our creations, we build connections. We overcome the language barrier and carry on a visual conversation,” explains Jude Ibrahim, the well-being coordinator, as Miguel asks for black paint in Spanish.
Les réfugiés et les demandeurs d’asile s: Refugees and asylum seekers face a new, overwhelming reality. It puts health and well-being services out of reach. “I’ve often noticed that people only talk about their mental state when it weighs on all of their daily functions and they can no longer, for example, sleep, or they have nightmares or incessant anxiety along with depressive and suicidal thoughts,” the coordinator reveals. “At first, they have too many things to worry about: the legal process, finding housing, finding a job. Mental health doesn’t matter at that point, because they’re too busy surviving in the most basic sense of the word,” she clarifies.
De nombreux bénéficiaires comme Miguel o: Many clients like Miguel were referred to the Ruche artistique by the legal assistance department, one of the most sought-after services. The well-being coordinator, aware of the importance of meeting the diverse needs of refugees and asylum seekers, stresses the pressing need for a cross-cultural approach. “Culture is like a pair of glasses: it shapes how we perceive symptoms, emotions and mental health. The way we feel these emotions can also vary from one language to another. That’s why it’s crucial to approach mental health with cultural humility,” Ms. Ibrahim explains passionately. She describes the difference between being culturally competent and being culturally humble. “Rather than imposing labels or diagnoses, it’s essential to empower people to define their own experiences and to provide them with support and resources that suit them. Ultimately, they are the experts on their own lives, and it is our duty to listen and help in a way that respects their culture.”
Elle souligne aussi qu’un accès adéquat: She also points out that adequate access to information is essential to dispel the feelings of confusion and despair that many refugees and asylum seekers may experience. The CDR offers group workshops, some aimed at helping people better understand health insurance, for example, and others focused on individual services so that people can meet with a social worker free of charge. Other workshops address the questions asylum seekers ask most often. In her work, Ms. Ibrahim structures the programs so as to “promote continuity, empowerment and the human dignity inherent in every individual, things that are often undermined throughout the migration process, particularly for asylum seekers.”
La Ruche artistique touche à sa fin, et: The Ruche artistique session is drawing to a close, and every seat around the table is now taken. Asylum seekers, refugees and citizens have joined the Ruche community; some have simply dropped in, while others are waiting for workshops and appointments. Miguel, meanwhile, scrapes the dried black paint with his key, revealing colourful cracks beneath a darkened sky. He gazes proudly at his creation, a symbol of his hope and his convictions: on one side, “God is love,” on the other, “Canada” and “Venezuela.” Meanwhile, Louis Salomon crisscrosses the city in search of a job and psychological support, trying to ease his distress.
Entre-temps, le chemin Roxham sera fermé: In the meantime, Roxham Road will be closed this Friday at midnight. Many people like Louis and Miguel are crossing jungles and borders right now in the hope of reaching safety. While this measure may reduce irregular migration, several experts fear it will in fact force migrants to take even more perilous routes, putting their lives at even greater risk.
